claims.text: Supply-side policy is the use of government measures to raise the economy's capacity to produce, by making workers more productive, removing barriers that hold firms back, and strengthening the incentive to work, save and invest.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Supply-side policy works on what the economy can produce, whereas monetary policy works on the cost of borrowing and the stock of money, and fiscal policy works on government spending and taxation; the three families of policy differ in the lever they pull.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Supply-side policy aims at the productive side of the economy over the long term: its measures raise output per worker and encourage new firms and investment, so the gains tend to build up over years rather than weeks.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The main supply-side policy measures are education and training, labour market reforms, lower direct taxes, deregulation, improving incentives to work and invest, and privatisation.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Education and training raise the skills of workers, so output per worker tends to rise and firms can produce more with the same workforce; labour market reforms, such as making hiring rules simpler, tend to make it easier for firms to take on workers and for job seekers to find them.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Lower direct taxes raise the reward from each hour worked and from each Namibian dollar of profit kept, so people tend to work and invest more; deregulation removes rules that raise firms' costs or block new entrants, so setting up a firm tends to become cheaper and quicker.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Privatisation moves a state-owned business into private hands, and its supporters expect keener attention to costs and customers; where a state-owned firm has no rival, the gain may go missing, since the private owner faces no other seller to compete with.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Supply-side measures tend to strengthen the economy's capacity over years, and the gains depend on the measure being carried out well: a training programme teaches little where the teaching is poor, and a tax cut may be saved rather than invested.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A supply-side measure that raises output per worker tends to serve the aim of economic growth, because the economy can produce more without needing more workers or machines; it tends to serve employment too, since workers who can produce more are often easier to employ profitably.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Supply-side policy bears on price stability through capacity: where firms can produce more for the same effort, pressure on prices tends to ease, and where the economy grows faster than demand, a rise in prices tends to slow.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Supply-side measures may serve one aim while working against another: lower direct taxes strengthen the incentive to work, but they cut the government's revenue and may force public spending down; the gains also arrive slowly, so a government facing a crisis now tends to reach for other policies first.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The macroeconomic aims supply-side policy serves are those of topic 4.2: growth in total output, employment, price stability, a sound external position and a fairer distribution of income; supply-side measures tend to work toward the first four through the economy's capacity to produce, while their effect on the distribution of income depends on the measure, since lower direct taxes may widen the gap between high and low incomes.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Labour market reforms include simpler rules on hiring and dismissal, better job-placement and vacancy information, help for workers to move to where jobs are, and more flexible working arrangements; they tend to make firms readier to hire and to shorten the time job seekers spend between jobs, though weaker job protection may reduce workers' security and bargaining power.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Improving incentives to work means making sure a person gains clearly from taking a job or working more, for example by withdrawing benefits gradually rather than all at once and by lowering tax on low earnings; improving incentives to invest means raising the return firms keep from new capital, for example through tax allowances on spending on new machinery.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.
